Error Catalog

Source: vignettes/error-catalog.Rmd
error-catalog.Rmd

中文版 →

This page lists the entry errors that the validation of the cleaning pipeline considers, so that a reader can see what was tested, where each error type comes from, and what the pipeline is expected to do with it. It holds counts and mechanisms only. It contains no participant identifiers and no row-level data.

The machine-readable source is validation/synthetic/error_catalog.yaml in the repository. This page and that file are meant to agree; if they do not, the file is the record and this page is out of date.

How the catalog is counted

The catalog has 17 entries:

  • 1 negative control (no_error_control): rows left untouched, used to measure false alarms.
  • 16 error types. Of these, 14 are injected in the committed synthetic benchmark (7,000 rows, 5,391 rows with an injected error, 1,609 clean control rows). The other two are not in that run: awake_misread_as_waso is documented but has no injector yet, and awake_is_getup is opt-in and was run separately (see below).

So “14 error categories” (README) and “15 categories” (the 2026-09-02 re-run described in Validation Methodology) are the same benchmark: 14 injected error types, and 15 when the clean control is counted as a category.

Where an error type comes from

Each type carries one or more of three tags. The tags matter because a benchmark built only from errors the project has already seen would measure the rules against the errors they were written for.

Tag Meaning
observed Seen in this project’s own data
literature Reported by a published sleep-diary study (SHUTi, RESTING)
blind_spot Possible in principle, and not caught by the pipeline until a dedicated check was added

The third source is the ordinary behaviour of someone filling in a form: a wrong AM/PM, a wake time given as the time of getting up, a clock time typed where a duration was asked for. Where a published study gives a rate, it is cited below. Where none does, the catalog says so and does not supply a number.

The error types

Clock times (bedtime, sleep onset, awakening, get-up)

Type What happens Source What the pipeline does
ampm_swap An evening time is entered with the wrong AM/PM, giving an apparent gap of 12 hours or more observed, literature Step 4 subtracts 12 hours when that restores a plausible order; otherwise the row goes to review
adjacent_swap_bed_sleep Bedtime and sleep onset entered in each other’s field, gap under 3 hours observed, literature Swapped back in Step 4
adjacent_swap_sleep_awake Sleep onset and final awakening exchanged, gap under 3 hours observed, literature Swapped back in Step 4
adjacent_swap_awake_getup Awakening and get-up exchanged, gap under 3 hours observed, literature Swapped back in Step 4
adjacent_swap_large_gap_left_clean An exchanged pair with a gap above 3 hours, which the swap rule deliberately leaves alone observed, blind_spot Left to the order check, which should flag it
compound_ampm_and_swap An AM/PM error and an exchanged pair on the same night observed, blind_spot The two rules each look at one pair, so the pipeline can blame the wrong field; this type measures that risk
awake_is_getup The rise time is typed in the wake-time field, so the two agree literature Equal times are valid, so this form cannot be told from a true entry. Opt-in; run as a stress test
awake_misread_as_waso A brief awakening in the night is given as the final awakening observed, blind_spot Documented only; no injector yet

Durations (sleep-onset latency, wake after sleep onset)

Type What happens Source What the pipeline does
field_misentry_sol A clock time is typed where the sleep-onset latency was asked for observed, blind_spot Step 1.5 checks for it; since 1.8.0 Step 6.5 also recomputes the latency when the typed time is close to the recorded sleep onset
field_misentry_waso A clock time is typed where the wake-after-sleep-onset duration was asked for blind_spot Step 1.5 checks for it; since 1.8.0 the value is set to missing when it looks like a clock time
format_no_colon A duration typed without a colon observed Read by digit count in the interval parser
format_malformed_colon Colons in unusual places observed Regrouped by pattern in the interval parser
mmss_confusion A short duration whose text can be read as minutes and seconds observed The MM:SS rule can read it wrongly; the entry is flagged for review
implausible_duration A well-formed but extreme duration, whatever the person’s own baseline literature Row-level thresholds in Step 8
cross_participant_spike A well-formed value far outside that person’s own usual range observed Step 8.5
sol_window_contradiction The reported latency does not fit between bedtime and sleep onset observed, blind_spot Flagged in Step 8

Control

Type What happens
no_error_control Rows are left as they are, to count false alarms and altered clean rows

Out-of-order nights, by mechanism

The four times of a night should satisfy bedtime ≤ sleep onset ≤ awakening ≤ get-up. A night that does not is out of order. Most of these are not two fields exchanged. In the study data, 140 of the 2,848 nights with all four times readable (4.9%) were out of order; 6 of the 140 have an unusable get-up value and are not an ordering problem, which leaves 134 (4.7%). By mechanism:

Mechanism Nights
Two fields exchanged 47
One field 12 hours from where it belongs 57
Two fields moved together by 12 hours 14
Awakening earlier than bedtime 6
All gaps within rounding (10 minutes or less) 3
Not explained by any single edit 7
Get-up value unusable 6

The package function classify_reversals() assigns each night to one of these and reversal_summary() counts them; Figure 33 plots the result. See the function help for the exact classes and thresholds.

In the study data the automatic rules repaired 89 of the 140 nights and human review the other 49. The rules handle a sleep-onset time 12 hours out and an exchanged pair almost every time. They handle almost none of the nights where the bedtime is 12 hours out or the whole night has moved; those need a person.

What the benchmark and the external rates show

  • With the committed synthetic benchmark, detection means “the row was flagged”, not “the value was recovered”. Correction is reported separately per type in the validation report.
  • Two published studies give rates that do not come from this project’s data. SHUTi reports 487 of 45,598 diaries (1.07%) needing a date or AM/PM correction. RESTING (3,382 diary-days) reports confusing wake time with rise time as its commonest entry error (150 diary-days) and 28 AM/PM errors. Two error mixes were built from these at 5% of rows and injected into this project’s own synthetic diary data. In the first, wake and rise are exchanged; every injected row was corrected. In the second, the rise time is typed in both fields; none was detected, because equal times are valid. The mean total sleep time that this could bias is bounded at about 0.8 minutes under stated assumptions. Clean rows were not altered in either mix.

Types that have no external rate

Most of the duration types (format slips, the MM:SS confusion, the spikes) have no published rate in sleep-diary studies. The catalog keeps the rate observed in this project’s own audit as an anchor and labels it as such. It is not offered as the rate in other data.

Where the pieces are

What Where
The catalog, machine-readable validation/synthetic/error_catalog.yaml
The injectors and the benchmark runs validation/synthetic/
The external-rate mixes validation/synthetic/prevalence_grid.R
The out-of-order classification classify_reversals(), reversal_summary()
The duration clock-time rule Step 6.5, duration_clock_rule in config_default.yaml
